accuracy.evidence: Advice follows the UK Department for Education relationships education guidance (online relationships, internet safety and harms), NSPCC and Childnet guidance for primary pupils, and the IB PYP PSPE interactions outcome: keep personal information private, people online may not be who they say, block and report, tell a trusted adult. It avoids scare claims and says children will not be in trouble for telling.

misconceptions.evidence: Tackles the common beliefs at this age: a school name or a uniform photo is harmless (step 1 card and step 5 post), mean comments or laughing emoji do not hurt on a screen (step 2 prediction and replies tagged mean, pile, emoji, joke), keeping a secret an online contact asks for (step 3 prediction and the secret tile), trusting a profile's stated age, and deleted posts being gone.

lab_distinct.evidence: flagnetsafe is the only lab built on a tablet: a private or shareable card sort, posts whose avatar flips to show the real child's face after a reply, a worrying message with safe and unsafe action tiles, friend-request profiles that reveal who is really there, and a growing digital-footprint trail. No other personal and social lab covers online life, and the shingle gate passed.

lab_teaches.evidence: Children act out each safety rule rather than read it: they decide what to keep private and hear why, feel the consequence of an unkind reply as the child's face turns sad, assemble stop, block and report, tell from five options, test friend requests against knowing someone in real life, and see each post they choose join a permanent footprint.

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions carry tempting wrong options: sharing a school name being harmless, mean comments hurting less online, and keeping a secret when told not to tell. Each is tested inside its step by the private bin explanation, the sad face behind the post, and the secret tile being rejected with the reason, and the done message reports the prediction.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Five rotating questions with ten tagged wrong answers (school, street, emoji, share, online, peer, deal, friendly, gone, only), each explaining the specific risk, such as friends sharing a post with people you do not know. In-lab feedback also names the slip, such as an address telling a stranger where you live, or a laughing emoji still hurting.

readability.evidence: The kid explanation passes the family FK limit in the validator, with short sentences and one rule per paragraph. The adult text stays inside the 10.5 limit and lists the key terms for ages 7 to 9. Lab cards are short phrases with an emoji, and every message is one or two plain sentences.

no_filler.evidence: Each kid paragraph gives one rule with a concrete example (what is private, a real reader, stop-block-tell, profiles and posts). Adult paragraphs give curriculum links, terms, named mistakes and what each lab step practises. Practice and mastery items apply the rules to fresh situations rather than asking for definitions to be repeated.

mobile.evidence: Checked screenshots at 360 px Android dark and iPhone 13 light for all six steps: the two bins and the draggable fact card fit one screen, three reply rows sit under the post, the five action tiles form a two-column grid with large tap areas, and the accept and say-no tiles are half-width. Show me finished every task on iPhone 13 in the browser gate.

accessibility.evidence: The browser gate's axe-core run found no WCAG 2.1 AA violations in light or dark theme on desktop or iPhone 13 and logged no console errors. Every canvas action has a labelled button twin (keep private, share, reply, safe move, accept, say no, post) and the canvas aria-label is rewritten with each result, and feedback uses words and faces as well as colour.
